title: 'Probably got away with that one': Latham after Wellington draw
excerpt: New Zealand, who were 70/5 on the opening day, also entered the final session of the final day at five down in the 2nd second innings
author: Cricbuzz Staff
body: Tom Latham conceded New Zealand had "probably got away with" one after Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips batted out the final session at the Basin Reserve to save the first Test against India. The New Zealand captain said the rearguard was a test his side had rarely faced in recent years, with Test matches now routinely finishing inside four days.

New Zealand had resumed on the final morning at 119 for 2, still a long way behind India's 720 for 9 declared. They lost Devon Conway, Rachin Ravindra and Tom Blundell before Mitchell and Phillips came together and saw off 43 overs. Shubman Gill called it off with an hour to play and the hosts at 239 for 5. Mitchell was unbeaten on 49 off 186 balls and Phillips on 26 off 126.

"It's slightly different when you're not necessarily worried about runs. It's more about time," Latham said. "But the way those guys were able to apply themselves and stick to their plans for a long period of time and ultimately get the draw... I guess that's one that we've probably got away with. They looked really clear, looked really calm, and it was a situation that we haven't necessarily been faced with for a period of time, to play in a slightly different way and adapt to what was required."

Latham was especially full of praise for Mitchell, whom he described as a player built for exactly this kind of situation. "He loves playing for this group, whatever format it may be, and I know he loves playing Test cricket. I think it's his favourite format, and he certainly showed that today," he said. "He's played some really important innings for us all around the world in different situations, whether it be attacking or defending. He's a guy for a bit of a crisis, and again he put his hand up today."

India's fast bowlers had sent down close to 50 overs each in the match. Gill admitted afterwards that the pitch had too little in it for another 10 or 15 overs to make a difference. Only 24 wickets fell across the five days, and Latham agreed the surface was not the Basin Reserve pitch New Zealand were used to. "It's probably not your traditional Basin surface that we've been presented with over the last few years," he said. "A traditional Basin wicket is where it keeps its pace and bounce, and we probably didn't see that from day two onwards. It's a little bit [of a] cliché, but it's about trying to adapt to conditions as best we can."

He also backed Gill's complaint that the ball had gone soft too early. "I think he's spot on in terms of the ball," Latham said. "Apart from day one, where the wicket probably had a little bit more in it, the ball tended to get soft. You get through those first ten overs with a new ball and things look slightly different, whereas the usual characteristic of grounds in New Zealand is that the ball stays a bit harder and probably swings for a little bit longer." On Gill's call to relax the saliva ban, though, Latham said the rules were "not necessarily up to me". He doubted there would be any change, given what the world had been through.

The draw knocked New Zealand from second to third in the World Test Championship standings, with a series against second-placed Australia to come. It also means the series will be decided at Hagley Oval from Friday. Latham argued that the result counted for more than it looked. "The introduction of the World Test Championship has put a lot of context into Test cricket," he said. "It was nice to come away with the draw here, and the importance of not just falling over and ending the game... draws become important as well."

Latham himself made a pair, but he said he wasn't concerned about his own form. "It's about trying to do my role as best I can, whatever that may look like," he said. "I certainly understand from an opener's point of view, it can be hard at times, and I try to stay reasonably calm in those moments. I've played a few Test matches now, and hopefully I'll be able to lean back on those experiences."
